t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: What Skill Scanning Is: Auditing Agent Capabilities
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: What Skill Scanning Is: Auditing Agent Capabilities
description: AI agents act through capabilities — skills, tools, MCP servers — and each capability is attack surface. Skill scanning is the discipline of inventorying what an agent can do: enumerate its tools, inspect each tool's declared schema and permissions, and compare against policy. The questions are simple and load-bearing: does the support agent need filesystem write? Does the research agent need the production database? Scanning turns 'the agent can do things' into an explicit, reviewable list.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: MCP Servers: The New Attack Surface
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: MCP Servers: The New Attack Surface
description: Model Context Protocol servers give agents standardized access to data and actions — files, databases, APIs — which makes them the agent ecosystem's plumbing and its newest attack surface. An MCP server with broad permissions is a confused-deputy risk: the agent can be tricked into misusing it. Scanning MCP servers means reviewing their exposed tools, their permission scope, and their input handling — the same rigor once applied to web APIs, now applied to agent plumbing.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Policy: Least Privilege for Agents
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Policy: Least Privilege for Agents
description: The policy states what each agent may do: which tools, which arguments, which data — the agent's job description as an enforceable document. Least privilege is the principle; the policy is its expression. Good policies are generated from observed behavior (the agent used these 5 tools in testing) then tightened by review. The policy is versioned, reviewed, and attached to the deployment — capabilities as configuration, not folklore.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Enforcement: The Runtime That Says No
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Enforcement: The Runtime That Says No
description: Scanning finds; enforcement prevents. The agent runtime interposes on every tool call: check the grant, validate arguments against the schema, log the invocation. A call without a grant is denied; a call with anomalous arguments is flagged. Enforcement must be in the runtime's trust boundary — a policy the agent can talk its way around is decoration. The denied-call log is itself a security signal.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Prompt Injection vs Tool Grants
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Prompt Injection vs Tool Grants
description: Prompt injection tries to make the agent misuse its tools; grants limit what misuse can achieve. The defense is layered: input sanitization and instruction hierarchy reduce the trick's success, but the grant boundary contains the blast radius when it succeeds. An injected 'delete the database' fails if the agent has no delete grant — the scanner's work pays off exactly here. Security is not preventing the trick; it is making the trick worthless.
key_facts: Defense in depth: prompt + grant layers

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Supply Chain: Skills from Strangers
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Supply Chain: Skills from Strangers
description: Agent skills increasingly come from marketplaces and third parties — convenient and risky. Scanning third-party skills means reviewing their code, their declared permissions, and their network behavior before granting anything. The discipline mirrors software supply-chain security: pin versions, review updates, monitor behavior. A skill update that quietly adds a network call is the agent equivalent of a compromised dependency.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Defensive Uses: The Governed Agent Fleet
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Defensive Uses: The Governed Agent Fleet
description: The defensive value is agents you can field: customer-service agents with chartered tools, research assistants with read-only grants, operations agents with dual-approval on actions. Each agent's charter is reviewed, its calls are logged, its grants expire. The fleet becomes manageable — hundreds of agents, each with a known, bounded capability set. Governance is what lets agents graduate from demos to infrastructure.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Cross-Agent Risk: Agents Talking to Agents
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Cross-Agent Risk: Agents Talking to Agents
description: Agents increasingly invoke other agents — and the composed capability can exceed any single charter. Cross-agent risk analysis maps the invocation graph: which agents call which, what the transitive permissions are, where the composition creates privilege escalation. The scanner that only sees single agents misses the system. Governance must cover the graph, not just the nodes.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Audit Trails: Proving What the Agent Did
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Audit Trails: Proving What the Agent Did
description: When an agent acts, the audit trail must answer: which agent, which tool, which arguments, which grant authorized it, what resulted. The trail is hash-chained and retained per policy — it is the evidence for incident review, compliance, and the occasional 'why did it do that'. An agent without an audit trail is an employee without a record: unmanageable at scale.
key_facts: Who, what, with whose grant, what resulted

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Debugging: The Denied Call
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Debugging: The Denied Call
description: The common operational event is the denied call: the agent tried something outside its charter. Triage is: was the charter wrong (legitimate need, grant it after review) or was the agent wrong (prompt issue, fix the instructions)? The denied-call log with full context — the prompt, the attempted call, the charter — makes the triage fast. Denied calls are the system working, not failing.
key_facts: Triage: fix the charter or fix the agent

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Continuous Monitoring: Drift in Capabilities
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Continuous Monitoring: Drift in Capabilities
description: Agents drift: new tools added, charters widened, temporary grants forgotten. Continuous scanning watches for drift — the weekly scan diffed against the charter, alerts on unreviewed changes. Temporary grants with expiry are the pressure valve; the monitor is the enforcer. Capability hygiene is maintenance, not a milestone.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Testing: Red-Teaming the Agent
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Testing: Red-Teaming the Agent
description: Agents are tested adversarially: prompt-injection suites, tool-misuse scenarios, and grant-boundary probes — the red team tries to make the agent exceed its charter. The grant layer must hold; the audit trail must record the attempts. Red-teaming is scheduled, not occasional: each charter change re-runs the relevant probes. An agent that survives its red team earns its deployment.

t: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Real-World Pattern: Support Agent Hardening
title: Cisco DefenseClaw / Skill Scanner: Real-World Pattern: Support Agent Hardening
description: A complete pattern: a customer-support agent starts with broad tools, gets scanned (12 tools, 4 unnecessary), chartered to 8, sandboxed, red-teamed, and deployed with expiring grants and full audit. Six months later the charter census catches scope creep; the grants are re-tightened. The agent serves a million conversations without a single out-of-charter action — governance as the enabler, not the obstacle.
